So inside containers, every Java request will re-hash the JDK, about 1.6 seconds, until #10380 lands. That issue will check each layer and includes a container measurement before the later 3d step.

I approved the first milestone of a new plan, G7, which reproduces CodeQL's two Rust pointer queries: use of a pointer after its lifetime ends, and access through an invalid pointer. Two points from it are worth knowing:

- **Parity target.** CodeQL's own expected results for the invalid-pointer test list 28 findings on 25 lines, but the campaign gate counts 21. I set the full 28 as the target. 21 counts as parity only if every difference is shown to be a scoring artifact of the gate.
- **Public interface.** The new behavior goes behind an optional profile parameter on the existing Rust pointer query, so current users see no change. The value names and the policy side belong to c43.

I also accepted #5658's plan to fix the cost blocker in the Python type-query switch. It reuses one request and one cache per query, the way Go already does. A few Python provider sites will stay on the old route until related work lands, rather than holding back the switch.

I withdrew my G7 interface ruling in favor of c43's design. Instead of a mode option on the existing pointer query, there will be two new query steps, one per relation, each named for what it checks. That fits the repository's own rule against mode parameters, and it leaves the existing query, which answers a different question, untouched. It needs no query-format version bump, because it only adds steps.

I kept one condition. CodeQL's lifetime query ignores pointers carried through closures, and so will these steps. When a closure could carry the pointer, the result must say closures were excluded, so that a clean result is not read as "no problem anywhere."

**The standard-library slowdown has its cause.** It came from #10186, the #10052 C# change that taught qualified-name lookup to find members whose names contain dots. That change replaced indexed exact-match queries with ones that split every stored name at its dots, so SQLite now scans tables where it used to seek. It hits every Rust policy run that uses the standard-library pack.

The issue is filed as bifrost-dev#10397, and I sent it to the owning session, 079c08c9 ("bifrost-dev via claude3"). A fix that keeps #10186's answers unchanged needs no cache token. I asked for query-plan evidence and a timing check on the regression fixture.

The #10399 plan surfaced a bug on master: taint run diagnostics are not deterministic. Which call sites a run refuses depends on the order threads finish. One repository gave 9 refusals on one run and 13 on another. I approved the fix, which ties each result's refusals to the lookups that result actually made, and required a test with shuffled thread order. bifrost3 measured that connecting the cache barely changed the cost. The expensive part is each lookup asking whether a call like `x.next()` constructs a class, which needs the type of everything before it. I confirmed its reading of my earlier rule: only a plain name path, such as `Foo`, `mod.Foo` or `self.Inner`, can name a class. A call on a computed value now skips that question entirely. This matches what legacy and the Rust and Go routes do, and if a class really is reached that way, the result is left open rather than wrong. Nothing here needs your decision.

Two things this round:

- **The Bat p8 re-measure ran.** 07d292ca's design work shows why Bat still reuses nothing. Saving is all-or-nothing per policy: one result that cannot be stored throws away the 29 good ones out of 42, and the fallback then recomputes all 42. I accepted a design that saves each good result on its own and recomputes only the unstable ones. It needs no cache token, because the final answer equals a full recompute. I required a test proving that equality, not just the argument. The estimated warm-run work on Bat drops from 84 computations to 26.
- **Another of David's PRs, #10427, took an ICFG pair I had reserved.** I moved the two affected unpushed PRs, #10146 and #10106, off it, and gave #7643 and #7860 fresh pairs above master. This is the same coordination gap I raised earlier.

I accepted #9737's way of making sure stale stored rows can never mark a crate as complete. Every query gets its list of crates from a component that re-checks the current version of the source-listing proof, so rows from the old version count as unknown. This avoids rebuilding every crate's route index whenever that proof changes. I required the rule to be enforced by a type, or failing that a source-scan test, rather than by convention. Nothing here needs your decision.
